Kuni no miyatsuko, also read as kokuzō or kunitsuko, were people in ancient Japan during the Yamato period who governed provinces called kuni. Kuni no miyatsuko governed provinces called kuni (国). At first Kuni no miyatsuko were appointed by the Emperor, but later the position was passed down from father to son. Kuni no miyatsuko had noble titles, usually kimi (君) or atae (直). But the important ones had the title omi (臣). The position was abolished in the Taika refoms and replaced with the position of Kokushi. The old kuni no miyatsuko were given the position of gunji instead. Gunji was a religious position responsible for Shinto in each province. These religious officials became known as shin-kokuzō, or "new" kuni no miyatsuko. The Gunji often supported the rights of peasants, so the position was abolished by the Emperor. A few kuni no miyatsuko families stayed powerful such as the of Izumo Province in present-day eastern Shimane Prefecture.

The Kupferhof Bauschenberg was a brass producing factory built in the 17th century in the German city of Stolberg. It had a great influence on the brass industry which made Stolberg world leader in brass production for more than a century. Due to the excellent conditions for the production of the alloy brass there could hardly be a better place to choose than Stolberg. Located near the small river Vichtbach the water wheels could easily be powerded. Calamine was delivered by the oar mines from nearby Breinigerberg and wood for firing the furnaces had been available in adequate quantities in the forests of the Eifel. This must be the reason why Gottfried Schardinel, one of the richest persons at that time in the region of Stolberg built the Kupferhof Bauschenberg. Later the three factories Kupferhof Bauschenberg, Dollartshammer as well as Straßburger Hof fusionated to create the company Prym. Karl Schleicher: Geschichte der Stolberger Messingindustrie. (=Beiträge zur Stolberger Geschichte und Heimatkunde, Heft 6, 1956, hsg. von der Stadtbücherei Stolberg (Rhld.)) {de}

The Kuremi Massacre was one of the chapters of the Anfal Campaign waged by the Iraqi regime against the Kurdish people in 1988. The massacre took place in the village of Kuremi in the Kurdistan Region, where residents were besieged, arrested, and many were executed en masse. This campaign was part of a broader policy of genocide targeting the Kurdish population, resulting in the deaths of thousands of innocent people. Despite the passage of years, the Kuremi Massacre remains a symbol of the tragedy endured by the Kurdish people under the Iraqi regime. Since the establishment of the Iraqi state in 1921, the Kurdish people have endured continuous oppression and marginalization by successive Iraqi governments. Kurdish regions in Iraq were subjected to policies aimed at erasing their cultural and geographical identity, in an effort to diminish Kurdish influence in those areas. Under the rule of President Saddam Hussein, these policies became increasingly violent, with the regime adopting practices of genocide and forced displacement. These policies aimed to eliminate the Kurdish identity and undermine any attempts to establish independence or autonomy in Kurdish regions. The Anfal Campaign, launched in 1988, was one of the most prominent episodes of repression faced by the Kurdish people. It involved the widespread use of chemical weapons and the systematic destruction of Kurdish villages. On August 27, 1988, the village of Korimi in the Kurdistan Region witnessed one of the most horrific massacres committed by the Iraqi regime during the Anfal Campaign, a genocidal campaign aimed at eliminating the Kurdish people in Iraq. Before the campaign, the village was home to about 150 Kurdish families, living a simple life in relative security. But this peaceful life soon turned into hell when Iraqi forces began their brutal campaign. When the villagers realized that the Iraqi attack was inevitable, they tried to flee towards the Turkish border in search of safety, but they were surprised by the border being closed by the Turkish border guards, leaving them trapped with no hope of survival. Their fate was certain death. About 300 villagers were arrested and separated from each other. The women and children were taken to the nearby village of Mankesh, while 33 of the men were taken to remote fields where they were shot. Only 6 of the men survived, but they were seriously injured and disfigured beyond description. The Iraqi soldiers were shooting them mercilessly, most of them even tried to escape, but were killed instantly by random gunfire. It didn't stop there, as the soldiers fired additional bullets into their heads to ensure they were killed once and for all. Those dark moments were more than just a massacre, they were a systematic genocide aimed at eliminating anyone who stood in the way of the regime. In the years that followed, mass graves were discovered containing the remains of many victims, including Fayez Taha Saeed, whose fate was confirmed by his wife after the discovery of the victims' clothes in 1992. This discovery was a confirmation of the loss of loved ones, as even after many years, the fate of thousands of victims remains unknown, and their families remain in a state of loss and dispersion. The survivors, however, went through another tragedy. After they managed to escape to the mountains, they lived for 11 days in tragic conditions, with no food or water other than what they were able to collect from wild grapes and water. Eventually, they were recaptured and taken to detention camps such as Baharka and Nazarka, where they suffered from hunger, disease, and torture. Women and children were separated from the men, and many of the men were sent to unknown locations where they are believed to have been killed in further liquidations. Following the 1991 Gulf War, survivors were relocated to the Kurdistan Region, but their suffering did not end. Many of them returned to their villages, but the memories of the massacre still haunted them, and the Koremi massacre remains one of the bloodiest chapters in the history of the Anfal campaign. Those dark days remain a witness to the brutality that befell the Kurdish people, leaving wounds that cannot heal and an indelible mark. The Anfal campaign caused massive destruction to the community of Koremi, with many innocent civilians killed, their homes and lands destroyed, and many families displaced. Survivors of the massacre suffered severe psychological and social repercussions, including the loss of family members and loved ones, as well as the destruction of their lives and futures. The Koremi massacre was part of the Anfal campaign launched by the Iraqi regime in 1988 with the aim of eliminating Kurdish identity in Iraq. This campaign included systematic genocide against Kurdish civilians, and was carried out using brutal methods such as mass executions of men and young men, forced displacement of families, and destruction of villages, in addition to the use of chemical weapons to destroy Kurdish villages and kill civilians. The massacre in Koremi was not just a normal military operation, but was part of a systematic policy to erase the Kurdish identity and destroy Kurdish communities in northern Iraq, making it one of the most heinous crimes against humanity committed by the Iraqi regime against the Kurds.

Fighting between the Kurdish people and the Turkish state has taken place since the fall of the Ottoman Empire, evolving into the present-day conflict sparked in 1984 fought between Turkey and the PKK. The conflict began with the creation of the Turkish state, whose policies turned the Kurds into an ethnic minority with few cultural and political rights. After Turkey was founded, uprisings begun in the Kurdish-dominated southeast, which were repeatedly crushed by the Turkish military. Decades of Turkey’s repression of Kurdish identity, especially after the 1980 military coup, boiled over in 1984, when the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) launched its armed insurgency against Turkey. The PKK wanted to create an independent Kurdish state, whilst Turkey focused on security and reaffirming its strong national character. The conflict has continued for years due to failed negotiations, broken ceasefire agreements, and shifting geopolitics.The PKK’s disbandment in early 2025 marked a promising step towards peace. Since 1984, there have been an estimated forty thousand deaths as a result of the conflict. The Kurds are an ethnic minority group who make up nearly a fifth of Turkey's population. Kurdish-Turkish tensions have existed for many years, but 1984 marked the violent escalation of the modern conflict, which has been a major challenge for the Turkish state. This conflict started with the collapse of the Ottoman Empire and the establishment of the Republic of Turkey, when the state tried to unite its diverse population under Turkish citizenship. The Kurds were harder to integrate than other minorities because they were concentrated in southeastern Turkey, were spread across national boundaries in Turkey, Iraq, Iran, and Syria, and were used to autonomous (independent) tribal rule during the Ottoman Empire. The loss of self-rule, forced assimilation, and repression of their culture by the Turkish state has fueled Kurdish nationalism since the Republic was founded. The Ottoman Empire was organized by millets, a system where different ethnic and religious communities had autonomy to self-govern in their own millets. Kurds, who are mainly Sunni Muslim, belonged to the Muslim millet, which included different ethnic groups. Communities within the millet were free to practice and express their separate cultures. During the time of the Ottoman Empire, groups were defined by their religion, not their ethnicity. This allowed the Kurds to maintain their distinct ethnic identity while being part of the Muslim majority within the empire. But by the late 19th century, the Ottomans started to embrace principles like nationalism and homogeneity, which gained prominence with the rise of nation-states.They applied these ideas by promoting uniformity, which began to weaken the millet system. After the Ottomans lost World War I, the empire was dissolved, and its leaders had to sign the Treaty of Sevres in 1920. This treaty would have given the Kurds the opportunity to establish their own state. But many Kurdish tribes actually allied with Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in his War of Independence, thinking it would help save the Caliphate. Atatürk, the founder of Turkey, also promised to establish a new state where Kurds would have political and cultural rights. In 1923, the Treaty of Lausanne replaced Sevres and its principles. Lausanne allowed the new Turkish Republic to be a unitary, secular (non-religious), and nationalist state. As a result, Atatürk did not keep his promise to the Kurds. By separating the state from religion, Turkey excluded Muslim communities who did not support this new system. With “Turkishness”, rather than Islam, as the main national identity, Kurds became minorities. This led to a strengthened sense of national identity as Kurds. The 1924 Turkish Constitution established that the country was not multinational, but a nation state, where the only nation that was recognized was the Turks. To create a “Turkish” state, non-Turkish identities had to be removed. Other minorities like Bosnians, Albanians, Georgians, and Circassians adopted a Turkish identity, but it was harder for the Kurds to conform, mainly because they were concentrated in the remote and mountainous southeastern region. Kurds were the largest minority group in Turkey, which allowed them to fight against Turkey’s policies against them. The Sheikh Said Piran rebellion in 1925 was the first revolt in the new Turkish Republic. Piran and other rebel leaders were against Turkey’s oppressive policies towards the Kurds. At the time, Turkey had been deporting Kurds, banning the Kurdish language, erasing mentions of the word “Kurdistan”, and attacking Kurdish villages. The revolt was crushed by Turkish forces, and Piran was executed along with the other forty six leaders behind it.The Sheikh Said rebellion united the Turkish population against such threats to the Republic, strengthening the nationalist government. In the aftermath, Atatürk could justify implementing his oppressive policies in a more aggressive manner. This rebellion took place in the Mt. Ararat region and was led by the rebels who survived the Sheikh Said revolt. At first, the Turkish government tried to negotiate with them, promising to pause deportations and give amnesty to the rebels, but neither side trusted the other. Turkey eventually resorted to indiscriminate (without distinction) air bombings which discouraged and weakened the Kurds. In the end, the rebellion was violently suppressed. The Turkish air force is credited for its major role in crushing Kurdish nationalist uprisings during this period. Under Ottoman rule, the Dersim region had been independent, and was even referred to as Kurdistan by the Ottomans. Oppressive Turkish rule led to growing anger among the Kurdish people of Dersim. In response, a local Kurdish leader named Said Rez sent his son to give a letter with demands to the Turkish government, asking the state to recognize the Kurds. The government arrested and killed Rez’s son, which sparked the Dersim rebellion in 1936. Because Dersim was closer to Ankara than the Mt. Ararat uprising, Turkey sent more troops and airplanes to crush the rebellion. However, the difficult terrain allowed the Kurdish rebels to outlast Turkish assaults. In the end, the rebels were finally crushed through a siege, which stopped food and supplies from entering. After the rebellion ended, Turkish officials claimed to have finally achieved a uniform Turkish national identity. The Kurdistan Workers’ Party, also known as the PKK, was created by Abdullah Öcalan in 1978. Öcalan was influenced by Marxist-Leninist ideology, his movement emerging during a period of radical leftist violence in Turkey. His aim was to establish an independent Kurdish state. In its early years, the PKK was not taken very seriously, not even by Kurds, and Turkey did not consider them to be a threat. At first, the PKK mainly fought against rival leftist and Kurdish groups, until they began attacking Turkish officials and military in 1984, reviving the conflict. The PKK is considered to be a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States, and several European Union countries. In the years before 1984, sustained violence between the Kurds and Turks had not been taking place. In fact, there were several moderate Kurdish organizations fighting for cultural and political rights. During the 1960s and 70s there was a rise of extreme leftist activism in Turkey. In response, the leaders of the 1980 military coup wanted to re-establish strong, unitary control over the country. They suspected Kurdish activists of working with the leftist extremists, so they cracked down on Kurdish organizations. The government arrested and tortured many Kurds suspected of activism and restricted Kurdish cultural expression. Without any legal or democratic avenues to advocate for their rights, many Kurds started to agree with the PKK. Once, the PKK was seen as a radical group, but after moderate Kurdish associations were crushed by the government, they became the only ones offering a pathway to freedom. The repression that followed the coup led many Kurds to flee to Europe, where they spread stories about Kurdish oppression under the new regime, as well as how the PKK was fighting for the Kurds. The existing Kurdish diaspora began supporting the PKK as a result. This was furthered by European countries condemning the backslide of democracy in Turkey and accepting Kurdish refugees. From Syria, Öcalan began to attack southeastern Turkey in August 1984. The PKK targeted military posts, state officials, and Kurdish elite who were working with the Turkish state. The PKK insurgency of 1984 were considered to be the largest rebellion against Turkey. The violence committed by the PKK resulted in a harsh Turkish response, further alienating (isolating) the Kurdish people from the state. In 1985, Turkey established the Village Guard to fight against the PKK. This group, made up of Kurds who opposed the PKK, helped to provide information and security to the Turkish military, but it also became known for its human rights abuses. By 1987, Turkey declared a state of emergency in the southeastern provinces, and when the conflict worsened in the early 1990s, the government renewed the state of emergency in 1992. This gave powers to the Turkish state to crack down on the civil rights of the Kurds and forcibly resettle the population. In 1993, the PKK declared its first ceasefire (an end to the fighting) after negotiations between Öcalan and Turkish President Turgut Özal. Unlike many Turkish politicians at the time, Özal believed that mistreating the Kurds would increase support for the PKK and threaten Turkey, and therefore wanted to find a democratic solution to the conflict. In response to the ceasefire declaration, Özal was prepared to make reforms, and took steps such as partially repealing Law 2932, which had banned the Kurdish language, and creating safe havens for Iraqi Kurds living under Saddam Hussein. But when Özal suddenly died in April 1993, Turkish authorities took the chance to attack the PKK again. The end of the ceasefire intensified the conflict and led to mass displacement of civilians. In the years that followed, Turkey invaded northern Iraq to attack PKK infrastructure, in Operation Steel (1995), Operation Hammer (early 1997), and Operation Dawn (late 1997). These resulted in the deaths of hundreds of PKK fighters and the destruction of many of their bases. As a result of the conflict, an estimated forty thousand people died, and millions were forced to flee southeastern Turkey. Both sides have invested billions of dollars into the conflict. Over time, Turkey’s counterinsurgency campaigns pushed the PKK into mountainous areas, decreasing the intensity of the fighting. The violence committed by the PKK in the early stages of the conflict shocked and alienated other Kurdish political groups, forcing the PKK to moderate its ideas to increase support. After Öcalan's arrest in 1999, the PKK abandoned its goal of an independent Kurdistan, instead focusing on securing cultural and political rights for Kurds within Turkey. From prison, Öcalan called for a democratic solution to the conflict and took responsibility for past mistakes, namely for the PKK targeting civilians. This period marked the end of the first insurgency that started in 1984. In 2004, the PKK restarted attacks against Turkey after declaring an end to the ceasefire. During this period, which lasted until 2007, the PKK carried out kidnappings and suicide bombings throughout Turkey. The years following Öcalan’s arrest were marked by cycles of peace and upticks in fighting, though with far less casualties than the first insurgency. For the most part, the PKK shifted from a military group to a political organization that was more open to negotiation. From 2012 to 2013, the PKK negotiated with Turkey, a process which invited another pro-Kurdish group, the People’s Democratic Party (HDP), to participate. The HDP had Öcalan’s support to unite the broader Kurdish movement and promote the peace process. It was also the first pro-Kurdish party to enter the Turkish parliament. However, progress slowed due President Recep Tayyip Erdogān’s policies, such as cracking down on the HDP, and the war in Syria in 2015. Many Turkish Kurds had gone to Syria to help fight against ISIS, which Turkey saw as an attempt to establish autonomous Kurdish rule, so it stepped away from the peace process. Furthermore, the 2016 coup attempt, which the PKK was not involved with, allowed Erdogān to go after Kurdish officials under the pretense that they helped to plan it. In recent years, Erdogān has been replacing pro-Kurdish officials with state-appointed ones, accusing them of terrorism and working with the PKK. Turkey continued to target PKK bases in northern Iraq through campaigns like Operation Claw, escalating the conflict and helping to strengthen Erdogān’s rule back home. Turkey’s operations in Syria during the Assad regime have also led to the displacement of tens of thousands of Syrian Kurds from their homeland, further diminishing the possibility of a united Kurdistan. On February 27 2025, Öcalan called for the PKK to disarm and disband. This declaration was welcomed by Turkey’s main political parties, including Erdogān’s party, the AKP. Iran and Iraq have also been supportive, hoping for more regional stability. Changes in the regional landscape, such as the overthrow of Assad and the loss of U.S. backing for Kurdish groups under Trump, put the PKK in a position where they could no longer continue their armed struggle. The PKK claimed that its mission was completed by having put enough pressure on Turkey so that the Kurdish issue could be solved democratically. That July, the PKK began disarmament, and withdrew forces by October. Further updates on the peace process have been slow and sparse. Negotiations are still in the early stages and could be derailed like they were back in 2015, especially if the PKK’s demands for civil rights and autonomy are not met. Meanwhile, the promise of ending the decades-long conflict could boost Erdogān’s popularity and support from Kurdish-aligned political parties, which he needs if he wants to further extend his presidency.

Kusunoki Masashige was a 14th century samurai from Kawachi Province. He fought for Emperor Go-Daigo. The warrior's conduct and death are recognized as examples of bushido. Kusunoki was a brilliant tactician and strategist. He defended two key Loyalist fortresses at Akasaka and Chihaya. This helped Go-Daigo to briefly return to power. However, one of the loyalist generals, Ashikaga Takauji, betrayed Go-Daigo. Ashikaga led an army against Kusunoki and the remaining loyalists. Kusunoki suggested to the Emperor that they hide on sacred Mount Hiei and allow Takauji to take Kyoto. Later, they could move quickly down from the mountain to trap Ashikaga and destroy him. Go-Daigo would not leave the capital. He insisted that Kusunoki meet Ashikaga's larger army forces in the field in a direct battle. Kusunoki obediently accepted his Emperor's foolish command. This became a great example of loyalty. He left his death poem with his young son Masatsura and knowingly marched his army into almost certain death. The battle took place at Minatogawa in modern-day Chūō-ku, Kobe. It was a tactical disaster. Kusunoki had only 73 of the original 700 horsemen left and was surrounded. He committed suicide along with his brother Masasue, 11 close clan members, and 60 others. According to legend, his brother's last words were Shichisei Hōkoku! (七生報國; "Would that I had seven lives to give for my country!") and Kusunoki Masashige agreed. Kusunoki Masashige's son, Kusunoki Masatsura, served the next emperor, the 12-year old Go-Murukami. These two had a trusting relationship like their fathers. Masatsura died alongside his brother Masatoki and cousin Wada Takahide in battle. That was the end of the Kusunoki clan. Kusunoki Masashige's successful defense of Chihaya castle is believed to have helped the emperor gain power against the Kamakura bakufu. Kusunoki held out so long in his castle, so Ashikaga Takauji changed sides and helped the emperor. The Kamakura bakufu ended. However, Ashikaga Takauji quickly learned that he did not like following the emperor's commands. He changed loyalty again and established his own Ashikaga bakufu. He was able to establish his own shogunate after defeating Kusunoki Masashige and the commander in chief Yoshisada in the final battle. Kusunoki Masashige tried to bring Ashikaga Takauji back to the emperor's side, but the emperor rejected this plan. Kusunoki's life and death are an important part of the historical narrative which is recorded in the Taiheiki.

The Kushan Empire was first formed in the early 1st century AD. It was located in Afghanistan, most of Pakistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and parts of northwest India. The Kushan were a branch of the Yuezhi or tibetian confederation. Previously a nomadic people living in eastern Central Asia, the Yuezhi moved southwest and settled in ancient Bactria.

Kvasir is a wise god in Norse mythology. He was made when the spit of the Vanir gods and Aesir gods was mixed after their battle. He became the new god of knowledge and diplomacy. Kvasir walked the world spreading his great wisdom to any who asked for it. He was killed by two dwarves, Fjalar and Galar, who mixed his blood with honey to make a powerful mead that inspired any who drank it to speak with wisdom and poetry. Odin drank all the mead to gain its knowledge. He spilled a few drops which fell into Midgard and was said to be the source of all the bad poets and artists. Odin is said to give the mead to those he feels worthy and this is the source for all the great poets. He is also considered to be the god of inspiration.

The Kven language is a Finnic language spoken in northern Norway by the Kven people. In 2005, the language was officially given minority status in Norway. This was for political and historical reasons. The European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages has rules for the signs of a minority language. Linguistically, however, it is seen as a mutually intelligible dialect of the Finnish language. Because of this it is grouped together with the Peräpohjola dialects, such as Meänkieli, spoken in Torne Valley in Sweden.

Kvens (Kven language/Finnish: kveeni, Norwegian: kvener, Northern Sami: kveanat) or Kven people are a Finnic ethnic minority in Norway. In the 9th century, king Alfred-the-great was told by Ottar, that kvens were a different people [or ethnic group] than Sami people or Finns. Kvens were paying taxes in Skjervøy, Norway, "five hundred years ago". The usual story [or traditional story], is that kvens are descendants from Finnish peasants and fishermen who moved from the northern parts of Finland and Sweden to Northern Norway in the 18th and 19th centuries. In 1996, the government of Norway officially said that Kvens were a minority group. In 2005, Norway officially made Kven language a minority language. As of 2024, some leaders of organisations for Kven people, have made accusations that Sami people have stole [parts of] the history of Kven people; Historians disagree with those new ideas; Norwegian authorities held back (for a while) some financing to a organisation for Kven people, because authorities did not agree with controversial ideas about history. In 2024, a report said that there were Kven people in Troms and in Finnmark in the 16th century; The report was written by Sannhets- og forsoningskommisjonen.

Kwik Save was a chain of stores in the United Kingdom which are closed down permanently since 2007. It was a discount store brand which offered own brand items for cheap prices in low-income places. It shut down because of competition from Asda, Tesco and Sainsbury's making their own cheap brands, and because of Lidl, Aldi and Netto becoming bigger and expanding in the UK. Kwik Save was brought back in 2012 by Costcutter. A lot of the old shops were sold to FreshXpress, a chain of stores similar to Kwik Save which also closed down in 2008, and the abandoned Kwik Save shops became popular to explore by urban explorers. Kwik Save was formed under the name Value Foods in Wales by Albert Gubay in 1959. Shops started being known as Kwik Save DIscount around 1967. Kwik Save was sold for $28 million in 1973 by Albert Gubay, and in 1998, Kwik Save merged with Somerfield.

Kyūdō is a Japanese form of archery. It is a martial art. Kyūdō is based on ancient archery (kyū-jutsu). Archery in Japanese began in the Jōmon period; and it developed in the samurai or military class. At the beginning of the Meiji era (1868-1912), the samurai lost their position because the Emperor Meiji replaced the Tokugawa family, the samurai, as a ruler of the nation. Therefore, all martial arts, including kyudo, declined. Before the Meiji Restoration, only the military class was allowed to do Kyūdō. But after it, ordinally people could also do archery, so it spread outside the military class and it became an amusement. Now, All Japan Kyudo Federation plays a role in the promotion of kyudo as a sport. There are many styles, but most of kyudo players are learning the technique ruled by All Japan Kyudo Federation (Shaho-Hassetsu). In most cases, style means the kind of movement (called Taihai). This is a major style and is known as the style of mannar. Most of the kyudo players play based on it. This style places importance on hitting and power. This style is derived from Heki style and Ogasawara style. This style is derived from Heki style. There are the Eight Stages of Shooting (Shaho-Hassetsu); which is a fundamental movement. Uchiokoshi; raising the bow straightly (Ogasawara and Honda style) or slantwise (Heki and Yamato style) Zanshin: "the remaining body or mind" or "the continuation of the shot" The equipment of kyūdō has evolved from ancient times. [[:Commons:Category:Yumi is the Japanese term for the bows used in kyūdō. Yumi is traditionally made of bamboo, wood and leather. But, recently, many yumi are made from fiberglass and carbon fiber. They are cheaper than those made of bamboo. Generally, there are two sizes. One is nami and the other is nobi. Nobi is longer than Nami. [[:Commons:Category:Ya is the Japanese term for the arrows of kyūdō. The arrow's shaft is traditionally made of bamboo. Recently, many shafts are made of aluminum or carbon fibers. The traditional fletching is made with three fins or vanes of eagle or hawk feathers. The modern ya may be made with turkey or swan feathers. People wear special clothes called Kyūdōgi when they practice kyudo or play a game. In a formal place, people wear Wahuku. [[:Commons:Category:Yugake is the glove worn on the right hand. It is typically made of deerskin.

Kōan was a [[Japanese era name after Kenji and before Shōō. This period started in February 1278 and ended in April 1288. During this time, the emperor|emperors were [[Emperor Go-Uda and [[Emperor Fushimi. 1281 (Kōan 4): Second invasion attempt by Mongol forces. This is called the Kōan War (Kōan no Eki). 1297 (Kōan 10, 10th month): In the 14th year of Go-Uda's reign, the emperor abdicated; and his cousin became the new emperor.

Kōra taisha is a Japanese Shinto shrine in Kurume, Fukuoka Prefecture. Kōra taisha was founded in the fifth century. It is mentioned in the Engishiki. It was the chief Shinto shrine (ichinomiya) of Chikugo Province and it is one of four in Fukuoka Prefecture. In 1915, the shrine was recognized in the system of State Shinto. It was one of six most highly ranked, nationally significant shrines or Kokuhei Taisha.

LGBT+ Labour, the Labour Campaign for Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual and Transgender Rights, is a socialist society related to the Labour Party in the United Kingdom. Originally called the Gay Labour Group, the purpose of this organisation is to campaign within the Labour Party and wider Labour movement to promote the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) peoples, and to encourage members of the LGBT community to support the Labour Party. 2015 marked the 40th anniversary of the organisation.
LGBT+ Conservatives is an organisation for LGBT conservatism in the United Kingdom. It is affiliated and is the official LGBT wing of the Conservative Party.

Lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) rights in the United Kingdom have improved a lot in recent years. In 2005, civil partnerships for same sex couples was legalised across the UK. In 2014, same sex marriage was legalised in England, Scotland and Wales. Gay people cannot get married in Northern Ireland because the Northern Ireland assembly voted against legalising it. Sex between two men was illegal in the UK until 1967, but no law was ever made regarding lesbian sexual activity. In 1967, sex between men was partially decriminalized in England and Wales. It was made legal for men over 21 years' old in 1967, with some very serious restrictions, legal for men over 18 in 1994, and equalized with the heterosexual age of consent in 2002. The bill in 2000 also introduced a lesbian age of consent for the first time too. In Scotland it was legalised in 1981 and in Northern Ireland it was legalized in 1982. However, the UK Parliament legislated for same-sex marriage in Northern Ireland, which is expected to come into force on or before 13 January 2020.

Lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) individuals in Jordan face legal challenges and discrimination not experienced by non-LGBT persons. In the Ancient times of Jordan, according to traditional Biblical accounts, Jewish scriptures and Islamic jurisprudence interpretations was the first place in the world where the same-sex activity was recorded in recorded times of human history, the story told by prophet Lot. However, until recently, the International Day Against Transphobia and Biphobia in 2014 and 2015 in the Jordanian capital, Amman, was troubling, primarily for educational purposes and for the community to raise voice and discuss challenges. Events were being held. LG GTT in Jordan Many activists and members of the Jordanian society and LG GTT allies attended. In 1951, an analysis of Jordan's Surgical Code legalized the legalization of private, adult, non-commercial, and voluntary physical laws. Jordan's penal code no longer allows family members to honour kill or maim any member of their family, which is interpreted as "Illegal" sexual intercourse in the whole family. By 2013, the newly revised Penal Code makes unlawful murder, unlawful killing legal. In 1999, a Jordanian family living in the United States repeatedly murdered their adult daughter and found out she was gay. Jordan was under the Ottoman Empire, where Homosexuality was condemned by the committee 75 years ago, but between 1922 and 1945, the country was ruled by a League of Nations. However, in 1951 the new nation legalized Homosexuality. The Jordanian government also tolerates a few cafes in Amman that are widely considered to be gay friendly. First, the content ban on "sexual perversion" has been replaced with a general requirement that the press "respect the values of... the Arab and Islamic nation" and that the press must also avoid encroaching into people's private lives.
